Hi Sam / Jenna —

Thanks again for the call today — appreciate the time and the clear color on FastPay's traffic profile. Quick recap and next steps from our side so we can line up the technical deep dive: 

Recap (what we heard)
- Latency targets: p95 end-to-end target ~200ms for streaming user-visible tokens; p99 acceptable up to 350ms for some back-office flows.
- Sustained throughput: ~150 qps for the payments orchestration flows.
- Concurrency/streams: ~200 concurrent streaming sessions under steady state.
- Burst profile: short spikes up to ~800–1,000 qps for 1–3 minutes during peak settlement windows.
- Streaming requirements: need server-side streaming (chunked) and partial tokens delivered as they generate.

Key qualification items we promised to validate / follow up on:
1) Autoscaling & burst handling — warm pools, scale-up times, and queueing behavior (how we preserve p95 SLO during bursts).
2) Concurrency limits & instance sizing — recommended concurrency per model instance given your model choice and prompt sizes.
3) Prefill/prefix caching opportunities — to reduce cold-token latency for highly-common prefixes in your flows.
4) Security/compliance docs we discussed (SOC 2 evidence) — Dylan will attach the standard pack.

Attachments: I've attached a short SLO_playbook and a sample autoscale-config.yml with our recommended warm-pool sizes for a starting point. Also attaching a draft proposal for your procurement team (proposal_FP-0421.pdf).

Next steps
- Technical deep dive (SRE + Infra): propose Tue/Wed next week (Mar 17/18) — 60 minutes. Dylan will lead the infra details.
- You share any historic qps traces (15–30 days preferred) and a list of the 10 most common prompt prefixes we can test cache-hit behavior on.

If anything above is off, please flag. Otherwise I'll schedule the deep dive and loop in our SRE (Dylan) and account lead (Dev).

Thanks Marissa — this is great, helpful recap. A couple clarifying items from our side before the deep dive: 

- Latency: our user-facing requirement is p95 <= 250ms (end-to-end), p99 <= 400ms for edge cases. The 200ms you called out would be ideal for some flows but not a hard requirement for all.
- Burst details: we see spikes historically around 700–1,000 qps lasting 90s–3m, typically once or twice per day during settlement windows.
- Concurrency: 200 steady streams is a good baseline. If the service starts queueing incoming streams during a spike, we need to understand expected queue lengths and whether we can surface a degraded UX (e.g., brief spinner) vs. failing requests.

Specific question for the deep dive: how quickly can Redwood scale to handle an unexpected jump from 150 qps to 1,000 qps? If a warm GPU pool isn't sized for the spike, what should we expect in terms of queueing and extra latency?

Also, can you confirm if streaming sessions are threaded to preserve partial tokens (i.e., no large buffering at the gateway) — that's critical for our UX.

Happy for the team to meet Tue (Mar 17) afternoon — please send proposed times.

Best,

Hi Sam / Jenna —

Thanks for the clarifying notes — good to have the explicit p95/p99 windows. Below is a concise summary of how Redwood would approach the autoscale + SLO guarantee given your profile, plus recommended config settings you can try in the POC: 

1) Fast-path: warm pools (recommended)
- Recommendation: maintain a warm pool sized to cover typical burst headroom. For your profile, we suggest a warm pool sized for ~600 qps sustained burst capacity (this covers the majority of your 700–1,000 qps spikes when combined with autoscale).
- Behavior: warm pool instances are kept 'pre-warmed' on the runtime (model loaded, KV cache primed optionally), so new sessions route to an in-memory instance with sub-100ms additional token latency.
- Expected scale-in/out time: warm-pool capacity is immediately available; adding new warm instances is a background operation (minutes) — so the pool is the primary mitigation for short 1–3 minute spikes.

2) Dynamic scale-up (cold-start path)
- If burst exceeds warm-pool headroom, Redwood will spin up additional instances. Typical cold GPU allocation + model load time is ~60–120s depending on model size and cloud region.
- During cold spin-up we use short-lived queueing with request prioritization: streaming sessions are accepted and placed in a short FIFO queue (default max queue wait configurable; we recommend 30–60s for low-failure UX).
- Queue behavior: prioritized streaming (interactive) requests are routed first; long-running batch requests can be deprioritized. Queue length impacts user-perceived latency — for example a 45s queue + token generation time will appear as ~45s extra. For your SLOs we recommend sizing warm pool to avoid queue waits for the majority of spikes.

3) Concurrency and instance sizing
- Recommended concurrency per instance depends on model and prompt length. For a mid-sized chat model (~7B), 6–12 concurrent streaming sessions per GPU gives a good balance; for larger Llama-2/Redwood-verified models, concurrency may be 3–6.
- For your target p95 <=250ms, we recommend starting with conservative concurrency (6/session for 7B), then stress-testing with your prompts and prefix caching to tune. Dylan will run a quick sizing matrix in the deep dive.

4) Caching & prefix strategy
- Prefix/KV caching is effective for payment flows that share common initial prompts. If you can supply the top 10 prefixes we'll evaluate cache hit-rate and estimate token latency reduction.

5) Streaming behavior details
- Server-side streaming: Redwood streams tokens to clients as generated; gateway buffering is minimal (we do not buffer full responses server-side by default). That preserves token-level UX.

6) Operational & monitoring guidance
- Alerts we recommend for POC: warm-pool utilization > 70%, queue wait > 20s, instance cold-start rate > 2/min.
- Rolling canary: we advise enabling a canary route for production to detect regressions in token latency after model/quantization changes.

Attachments: sample autoscale-config.yml (warm-pool sizes + queue TTLs) and the SLO_playbook — both attached. I also attached a draft proposal for procurement.
